title: Feeling blue
caption: The blue compact dwarf galaxy ESO 338-4, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: ESO 338-4 · constellation Sagittarius · about 100 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Young blue stars sit inside a cloud of dust and gas at the center of this Hubble image of ESO 338-4. It is a lonely dwarf galaxy about 100 million light-years away in the constellation of Sagittarius, the Archer, and it belongs to a class called blue compact dwarf galaxies.

Galaxies of this type are named for the intensely blue star-forming regions often found in their cores. One such region lies within ESO 338-4, full of bright young stars that are burning through hydrogen at a furious rate. They are massive, and despite their huge fuel supplies the reactions in their cores will use it up in only millions of years, a very short time by astronomical standards.

The young stars are the product of a recent merger between ESO 338-4 and a wandering galaxy. That encounter stirred up the surrounding clouds of gas and dust and set off a rapid burst of new star formation.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.89 x 2.04 arcminutes) and distance (100 million light years), the frame spans roughly 55,000 × 59,000 light-years. Its light set out about 100 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, Advanced Camera for Surveys and Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph observed the galaxy in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Parts of the data were taken in ultraviolet and infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint to see without a telescope.

explore: The image is credited to Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, and the observations also used the Advanced Camera for Surveys and the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph. Filters span ultraviolet light at 127 and 152 nanometers, visible light near 500 and 550 nanometers, and near-infrared light at 1.1 micrometers.
alt: A small galaxy with young blue stars in a cloud of dust and gas at its center.
